newsitem.title: INDIA: Leaders seek new ways to end sex bias in politics.
newsitem.headline: Leaders seek new ways to end sex bias in politics.

text.p: World leaders on Saturday pressed a 77-nation conference on women's empowerment to seek new ways to bridge a glaring gender gap in politics.
They called for the private sector to step in to correct a social bias that has so far stirred only activists.

"Without the inclusion of women in decision-making, real development cannot in fact take place, and cooperation and understanding between the sexes will remain a pipe dream," Namibian President Sam Nujoma told the conference.
Some 250 lawmakers from across the world are taking part in the five-day conference, organised by the Geneva-based Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).
The meeting, which began on Friday, is expected to adopt a declaration on Tuesday after debating strategies to increase the number of women in parliaments around the world.
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said society still treated women leaders as exceptions.
"Political life is still dominated by the privileged and powerful and, therefore, largely by men," she said.
Among other issues, delegates at the conference will discuss financing electoral campaigns and job quotas for women in legislatures.
United Nations assistant secretary-general Angela King told the meeting that women were consistently under-represented in power structures all over the world.
The IPU said this week that the share of women among parliamentarians had dropped to 11.7 percent from a high of 14.6 percent in 1988.
The group, which surveyed 1,000 political parties and 179 parliaments worldwide, said only one out of 10 party leaders was a woman despite a large number of female activists.
King said most discussions on womens empowerment took place among "the converted" -- womens political groups, feminist scholars and female politicians.
"We must involve male politicians, we must mobilise the private sector and we must reach out to women who have been too busy struggling for daily survival to be involved," King said.
Delegates urged the conference to build on the momentum created by the 1995 United Nations Conference on Women in Beijing, where some 40,000 participants from 180 countries discussed women's rights.

"Where half of the population are women and the majority are poor, the participation of women and the poor in politics has to be integrated in such a manner as to make democracy truly meaningful," Hasina said.
Former president of Iceland Vigdis Finnbogadottir said the U.N. meeting was proof that the women's movement had matured.

"We are not talking about winning a privilege from men and taking it over for ourselves, but rather about how society and humankind will gain fulfilment if these traditional barriers are abolished," she said.
Only six nations -- Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, North Korea, Nepal and the Philippines -- have laws stating that national legislatures must include a minimum percentage of women, the IPU study said.
Even in these nations, the share of women in parliaments was far below the proportion of women in the population, it said.
